_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: Everyone substitutes: [saying of] a non-sacred animal, “This one is in place of that one” of consecrated property.
rashi:a1.2: Not that a person is permitted to substitute: since it is written: “He shall not … substitute.”
rashi:a1.3: It is substituted: for he applies sanctity to it, and both of them are sacred.
rashi:a1.4: And he incurs the forty: on account of the prohibition “He shall not substitute.”
tosafot:a1.1: Everyone substitutes, both men and women: In [the mishna] “Everyone slaughters” [Ḥullin 2a] it does not teach “both men and women.” And the Gemara [here, 2b] explains why: since the whole passage is stated in the masculine, a verse was needed to include women.
tosafot:a1.2: And he incurs the forty: And if you say: why does it not teach eighty, since it is written (Leviticus 27:10): “He shall not exchange it, nor substitute it” [two prohibitions]? One can say that it does not come to give the number of lashes, but means only that he is flogged for it. And one can further say that in fact he is flogged only forty, and the two prohibitions are both needed: one for his own offering and one for another’s, for example where [the owner] said: Whoever wishes to substitute, let him come and substitute.
rashi:a2.1: Not that a person is permitted … after the fact: [this is said] in astonishment. [The clause implies] that ab initio one is not permitted to substitute, but after the fact it is fine.
tosafot:a2.1: In brief: How does the questioner know that “Everyone substitutes” means ab initio, when it might mean after the fact, as the parallel question at the beginning of Ḥullin (2a) asks? It must mean ab initio, for otherwise why would the mishna say “after the fact” twice; Reish Lakish argues the same about “Everyone slaughters” there. Rashi explained in Ḥullin that “twice after the fact” is no difficulty here, because the latter clause adds that he incurs forty lashes, though one might have thought a prohibition without an action carries no lashes. But on his explanation, what is the Gemara asking here? One cannot say that this is its answer, since the wording does not imply it, and then the answer would add nothing to the question. Rabbeinu Tam explains that the mishna uses strong language, “Everyone substitutes,” to teach that the substitution takes hold even when done intentionally, lest one say: forty lashes on his shoulders, and [the original stays] valid; and that is the Gemara’s answer. But below it says “it shall be” includes the unintentional like the intentional, implying that the intentional case is the more obvious. Rabbeinu Barukh answers that that teaching is about lashes; Rabbeinu Shimshon of Sens disagrees, since there are no lashes for an unintentional act. The texts differ on this below (17a): some read “with substitution he is flogged, with consecrated animals he is not flogged,” and some read “with substitution it is sacred, with consecrated animals it is not sacred.” Others say “it shall be” refers to the sanctity taking hold, since consecration in error is generally not consecration, so the intentional case is the more obvious; and the novelty of the intentional case here concerns sacrifice, since it says below that the substitute too is sacrificed, and the mishna teaches that it is sacrificed even when substituted intentionally. None of this seems right to the Ri, since Rav Yehuda’s answer, “Everyone can apply by substitution, both men and women,” would have no reason to mention men and women. So the Ri explains that the mishna uses the strong language “Everyone substitutes” because of women: the whole passage is in the masculine, and “hamer yamir” comes to include women, so one might have thought that both the exclusion and the inclusion take effect, the inclusion making a woman’s substitute sacred and the exclusion keeping it from being sacrificed. Therefore the mishna says “Everyone substitutes”: a woman’s substitute is sacrificed like a man’s. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
rashi:a3.1: Nor substitute it: and yet the mishna teaches that everyone substitutes, even ab initio.
rashi:a4.1: This is the reading: “Rather, this is what it is teaching: Everyone can apply [sanctity] by substitution, both men…,” etc. That is, the sanctity of substitution takes hold of an animal whether by the word of men or by the word of women. And this implies after the fact: that if she substituted, the sanctity of substitution takes hold even by a woman’s word; “but not that a person is permitted to substitute,” etc.
gershom:a1.1: Rav Yehuda said: This is what our mishna teaches: “Everyone substitutes” [means] they apply [sanctity] by substitution: everyone who said, “Let this be in place of that,” this one takes hold in place of that one. That is the meaning of “Everyone substitutes,” and it does not imply that they substitute ab initio. And therefore it teaches: “Not that a person is permitted to substitute” [that is, although everyone applies sanctity, it is not that a person is permitted to substitute] ab initio.
gershom:a2.1: “Everyone,” to include: that is, what did it leave out, that it did not teach?
rashi:a5.1: An inheritor: who substituted for an offering his father had set aside in his lifetime; his substitute is a substitute.
gershom:a3.1: To include an inheritor, who substitutes.
rashi:a6.1: An inheritor places hands: on his father’s offering, which his father set aside in his lifetime and did not manage to sacrifice before he died.
rashi:a7.1: What is the reasoning of Rabbi Yehuda: who said that an inheritor does not substitute.
rashi:a7.2: This is the reading: “He derives the initial consecration from the end of consecration”: he derives the beginning of consecration, such as substitution,
rashi:a7.3: from the end of consecration: that is, placing hands, which is close to the slaughter. And if you find it difficult that in Tractate Nazir (31a) substitution is called the end of consecration: that is because there it does not discuss placing hands at all, so substitution is the end of consecration relative to the offering for which it was substituted, since that offering is first and its exchange is second. But here, where we are speaking of placing hands, substitution is the beginning of consecration relative to placing hands, which comes at the end, immediately before the slaughter.
tosafot:a7.1: The initial consecration: such as substitution; from the end of consecration: that is, placing hands, which is close to the slaughter. And the reason substitution is called the end of consecration in Tractate Nazir (31a) is that there we do not speak of placing hands at all, so substitution is the end of consecration relative to the offering for which it was substituted, since that offering is first and its exchange second. But here, where we speak of placing hands, substitution is the beginning of consecration relative to placing hands, which comes at the end, immediately before the slaughter. [This is] Rashi’s wording.
gershom:a4.1: Rabbi Yehuda juxtaposes the beginning of consecration, that is, substitution, which one now brings into consecration, so that substitution is a beginning in consecration, with the end of consecration, that is, placing hands, which is immediately followed by slaughter; that is the end of consecration, for when he slaughters it the consecration is complete. Just as at the end of consecration an inheritor does not place hands, as it is written “on the head of his offering,” and not his father’s offering, so too he does not substitute. And my teacher told me that in Tractate Nazir (31a) as well, the beginning of consecration means the offering itself and the end of consecration means its substitute; the reason is that there it does not discuss placing hands, while here it does, so the meaning is as we said. And as for the Rabbis [that is, Rabbi Meir’s view], who hold that an inheritor places hands: isn’t “his offering” written, which implies an exclusion, that is, his offering and not his father’s offering? The Rabbis hold: three [times] “his offering” are written about placing hands with the peace offering: [one excludes] a gentile [the printed text here also reads “and not his father’s offering,” which seems out of place], since a gentile’s offering does not require placing hands; and [one,] not another’s offering, since a person does not place hands on another’s offering.
rashi:a8.1: From where do we [derive it]: that an inheritor does not place hands.
rashi:a8.2: “His offering” is written three times: with the peace offering, in Parashat Vayikra, from “And if his offering be a sacrifice of peace offerings” until “And if his offering be a goat,” and in all three placing hands is written.
tosafot:a8.1: His offering, and not the offering of a gentile: And if you say: why is “his offering” needed for this? It is already derived from “the children of Israel … and he shall place”: the children of Israel place hands, and gentiles do not. One can say that it is needed, lest you say that the gentile himself does not place hands on his offering, but the priests place hands on it instead; therefore “his offering” is needed, to say that a gentile’s offering has no placing of hands at all.
rashi:a9.1: Isn’t “his offering” written: which implies that he places hands on his own offering, and not on his father’s offering.
rashi:a9.2: Joint owners in placing hands: that if two or three became partners in one offering, we call it “his offering” for each and every one of them, and all of them place hands on it.
gershom:a5.1: All joint owners in placing hands: that if two or three brought one offering, all of them place hands on it, since for each one we call it “his offering.” And he holds that an inheritor places hands, since his father’s offering is like the inheritor’s own offering.
rashi:a10.1: He does not accept it: certainly it does not require placing hands [by each owner], since their offering is not specific; that is, since it does not wholly belong to each one. And when the verse is written, it is for “his offering, and not his father’s offering.”
gershom:a6.1: And Rabbi Yehuda does not accept all joint owners in placing hands: so one “his offering” remains for him to exclude the inheritor.
rashi:a10.2: Derived from one verse: which implies: his offering, and not [one who acts] as an agent [on another’s offering], whether of a Jew or of a gentile. For to exclude the gentile himself from placing hands no verse is needed, as we say in Menaḥot (93a) and in Torat Kohanim: “The children of Israel … and he shall place”: the children of Israel place hands, and gentiles do not place hands.
rashi:a10.3: And one remains for him, etc.: and there still remains the third “his offering”: his offering, and not his father’s offering, [for it might have entered your mind] that his father’s offering is not like another’s but like his own.
gershom:a7.1: And if you wish, say: in fact he accepts that it includes all joint owners. And from where does he derive it? Doesn’t he use one “his offering” to exclude the inheritor, one to exclude a gentile’s offering and one to exclude another’s offering? No: Rabbi Yehuda derives another’s offering and a gentile’s offering from one verse, since neither of them is his own; one remains for him to include all joint owners.
tosafot:a11.1: And what is the reasoning of Rabbi Meir, who said an inheritor substitutes: And if you say: why is a reason needed for Rabbi Meir? Since he does not expound “his offering, and not his father’s offering,” he evidently holds that an inheritor places hands, and if so he should derive substitution from it, since we derive one from the other. One can say: were it not for the verse “hamer yamir,” which includes the inheritor, he would have had to interpret “his offering” as excluding the inheritor rather than as including all joint owners. But now that “And if he shall at all substitute” is written to include the inheritor, who [therefore] places hands, he interprets “his offering” as including all joint owners. And if you say: why are the other mentions of “his offering” exclusions and this one an inclusion? One can say that you cannot read it as an exclusion, for then the verse could have been silent, and it would follow by itself that partners do not place hands, just as it says below (13a) that partners do not substitute.
rashi:a11.1: To include the inheritor: since it could have written: “And if he shall substitute animal for animal” [with the verb once]. “Hamer yamir”: for what halakha? To include the inheritor, that his substitute is a substitute.
rashi:b1.1: This is the reading: “And he derives the end of consecration from the initial consecration,” etc.
rashi:b2.1: The woman: that her substitute is a substitute, and she is flogged on account of the prohibition “He shall not substitute.”
rashi:b2.2: Only in the masculine, as it is written: “He shall not exchange it [lo yaḥalifenu]”: which is the masculine form; it is not written lo taḥalifenu, which would be the feminine form.
rashi:b2.3: What will we ultimately include, etc.: that is, from where will we learn that we are ultimately to include the woman? [Rashi’s text of the baraita reads “What will we ultimately include” where the printed text, and the Davidson English, have “from where is a woman derived.”]
rashi:b2.4: The verse states: “And if he shall at all substitute”: since the verse writes [the verb] twice.
gershom:b1.1: What will we ultimately include? The woman. That is, from here we learn that we are ultimately to include the woman, that she effects substitution: the verse states “hamer yamir,” it included [her]. [And the Rabbis derive the woman from “and if”: from the vav of “and if,” which is superfluous and need not have been written.] [Rabbeinu Gershom’s text, like Rashi’s, reads “What will we ultimately include”; by “the Rabbis” he means the view the Gemara gives as Rabbi Meir’s.]
rashi:b3.1: And according to Rabbi Meir: who needs “And if he shall at all substitute” to include the inheritor: from where does he derive a woman?
rashi:b3.2: He derives it from the vav: since it could have written “If he shall at all substitute,” and it writes “And if.”
rashi:b4.1: She is not flogged: [that is,] if she substituted, her substitute is not a substitute.
rashi:b5.1: And it answers; this is the reading: “These matters apply to a prohibition that involves an action”: in these punishments they are equal to one another, since it is written “shall commit [ya’asu],” which implies punishments involving an action, such as desecrating Shabbat and other prohibitions that involve an action. But for a prohibition that involves no action, such as substitution, which depends on speech alone, I might say she is not flogged. It teaches us [otherwise]. [Rashi’s reading differs from the printed text and the Davidson English, which follow the version he gives next.]
rashi:b5.2: Another version, written in the books: “These matters apply to a punishment that is equal for an individual and for the public”: in such a punishment they were made equal to one another. But here, with substitution, the public does not effect substitution, as we say in the other chapter (13a), and it derives this from the tithe.
gershom:b2.1: These matters, that the verse equated a woman with a man, are with a punishment that is equal for all, both for an individual and for the public; but here, since it is a prohibition that is not equal for all, as we learned: The public do not, etc. Another version: one might have thought these matters, that it equated a woman with a man, are with a prohibition that involves an action; but one who substitutes does no action, only speech, so I might say she is not flogged. It teaches us [otherwise].
rashi:b6.1: Who has not reached the age of vows: for example, less than twelve years old. For so we say in Tractate Nazir (62a): “A man, when he shall clearly utter [yafli]”: what does the verse teach? For it could have written “A man, when he shall vow a vow.” Rather, it comes to include a discriminating minor [mufla] near manhood, for example twelve years old: since he knows how to discern in whose name he vowed and in whose name he consecrated, his vow is a vow and his consecration is consecration. Younger than that, even if he knew to whom he vowed and to whom he consecrated, his words are nothing. Older than that, for example thirteen years old, even if he does not know in whose name he uttered it, his acts are acts.
gershom:b3.1: Who has not reached the age of vows: [that is,] twelve years, when his vows are examined.
rashi:b6.2: He cannot consecrate: as I explained above, that his words are nothing.
rashi:b6.3: Can he effect substitution: [said] in astonishment: so that he would be flogged?
rashi:b6.4: Who has reached the age of vows: that he is twelve years old, of whom we say there [in Nazir] that his vows are examined: if he knows in whose name he uttered it, his acts are acts, and if not, not.
gershom:b4.1: A discriminating minor: who knows in whose name he vows; for it could have said, “A man, when he shall vow a vow by your valuation”; what does the verse teach with “when he shall clearly utter”? etc. From the fact that he consecrates: a discriminating minor near manhood, who vows, that is, consecrates.
rashi:b7.1: He is not subject to punishments: until thirteen years.
rashi:b7.2: It is not applied: substitution does not take hold through him, since it is written: “He shall not exchange it, nor substitute it … then both it and its substitute [shall be holy].” That is, whoever is included in “He shall not exchange it, nor substitute it,” such as one subject to punishments, is also included in “then both it and its substitute shall be holy,” so that he applies [sanctity] by substitution. This excludes a minor, who is not subject to punishments.
rashi:b8.1: And even if you say that a minor can effect substitution, etc.: it comes to teach us a further novelty [about a gentile], and not because that is so [of the minor].
rashi:b8.2: From the fact that he can consecrate: for we include [this] in Menaḥot (73b): “Any man [ish ish] of the children of Israel … who brings his offering”: and we say: What does the verse teach with “ish ish”? To include gentiles, who vow vow offerings and gift offerings like a Jew.
gershom:b5.1: As it is taught: “Any man [ish ish] … who brings his offering, for any of their vows”: to include gentiles.
rashi:b8.3: He will not come to be subject to punishments: for a gentile is never flogged, but a minor comes to be subject to punishments when he is thirteen years and one day old.
rashi:b9.1: One may not derive benefit, and they are not subject to misuse: if one derived benefit from them he does not bring an offering for misuse, since we do not judge it like other consecrated property, where one who benefits from it has misused it; for it is forbidden for benefit only by rabbinic law, as below.
gershom:b6.1: Consecrated animals of gentiles: sacrifices that gentiles consecrate. One may not benefit from them, and they are not subject to misuse; it explains this below.
rashi:b9.2: And one is not liable for them, etc.: as it concludes below.
rashi:b9.3: And one does not bring, etc.: this is the reading: “And one does not bring libations,” and we do not read “for them.” And this is its explanation: one does not bring libations of gentiles by themselves, as a Jew donates libations by themselves; but together with his offering one brings them. As we say in Tractate Shekalim (7:6), this is one of the enactments the court enacted: a gentile who sent his burnt offering and the money for its libations from overseas, one accepts it from him. But his offering certainly requires libations, for together with his offering one brings libations. [The Aramaic printed on the daf does read “for them”; the Davidson English follows Rashi’s explanation.]
tosafot:b9.1: And one does not bring libations: Rashi explained: one does not bring [libations] of a gentile by themselves, as Jews donate libations by themselves, but together with his offering one brings them. As it says in Tractate Shekalim (folio 11, column 4) that this is one of the enactments the court enacted: a gentile who sends his burnt offering and the money for its libations from overseas, one accepts it from him. But his offering certainly requires libations, for together with his offering one brings libations from public funds.
gershom:b7.1: And one does not bring libations for them: [A printed note refers to Tosafot on Menaḥot 73b, which cites Rabbeinu Gershom’s reading here, “for them.”] According to this version it implies here that gentiles do not bring libations from their own for their offerings. And what we learned in Tractate Shekalim, that a gentile who sent his burnt offering from overseas and sent its libations with it, they are offered from his, is a rabbinic enactment, for the court enacted seven things and this is one of them; it is not Torah law. And according to the version that reads “one does not bring libations by themselves,” it means that they may not donate libations without a sacrifice, but their offering requires libations, either from their own or from public funds, as derived from “for any of their vows,” as is explained in the chapter Ve’elu Menaḥot. [A printed note adds that Menaḥot there implies that libations brought with the sacrifice need no verse, since they are part of the burnt offering and its accompaniments, and that the matter requires study.]
rashi:b10.1: With regard to all of them I see fit to be stringent: that one may not benefit from them, and they are subject to misuse, and one is liable for them on account of piggul, notar and impurity, like other consecrated property; except for the libations, which certainly one does not bring.
rashi:b10.2: In what case is this said: it goes back to the first tanna’s statement, and this is what it says: Where is the first tanna’s ruling, that one is not liable for misuse, said? With a gentile’s offerings for the altar.
rashi:b10.3: But with property consecrated for Temple maintenance: which a gentile consecrated, one is liable for misuse. Tractate Zevaḥim explains the reason, in the chapter Beit Shammai (Zevaḥim 45a); and some have this reading here in Temurah as well, below.
tosafot:b10.1: In what case is this said? With altar offerings; but with property consecrated for Temple maintenance one is liable for misuse: Rashi explained that we have come [back] to Rabbi Shimon. And the Ri explained that it is the conclusion of Rabbi Yosei’s statement, and this is what it says: Rabbi Yosei says: In all of them I see fit to be stringent; and as for what Rabbi Shimon said, that one is not liable for misuse with them, in what case is this said? With altar offerings, etc. And the Tosefta implies as Rashi explained, for it states there explicitly: But with property consecrated for Temple maintenance, Rabbi Shimon concedes.
rashi:b10.4: In any event it teaches: that the consecrated animals of gentiles do not effect substitution; so resolve [the dilemma] from this.
tosafot:b10.2: In any event it teaches: they do not effect substitution: And if you say: perhaps [Rami bar Ḥama] raises the dilemma according to Rabbi Yosei, who said he is stringent in all of them? One can say that he prefers to frame the dilemma so that it holds according to Rabbi Shimon too. Or one can further say that the dilemma necessarily cannot be framed according to Rabbi Yosei: since he holds that they do effect substitution, then even if you say that this is through a Jew, and Rami bar Ḥama asks whether the gentile himself can do it, you cannot say this. For necessarily, if a Jew applies the sanctity, the gentile must have said: Whoever wishes to substitute, let him come and substitute; and if the gentile himself does not effect substitution, how could it be done at all [literally: how could one make a burnt offering]?
rashi:b11.1: He said to him: in the case of the consecration of gentiles: that is, if it is because of this, there is no proof, for from here nothing at all can be resolved: [it speaks] where a gentile consecrated for a gentile to achieve atonement, that he set it aside for his own atonement. [Rashi’s text reads “He said to him” here.]
rashi:b11.2: I do not raise a dilemma: that his consecrated animal does not effect substitution, since he will not come to be subject to punishments.
rashi:b11.3: And a Jew achieves atonement: that a gentile set it aside for a Jew, so that the Jew would achieve atonement with it.
rashi:b11.4: Do we follow the one who consecrated: and the one who consecrated is a gentile, who will not come to be subject to punishments, and so does not effect substitution.
rashi:b11.5: Or the one achieving atonement: who is a Jew, and is subject to flogging.
gershom:b8.1: In all of them to be stringent: that they are subject to misuse, and one is liable for piggul, etc. But with property consecrated for Temple maintenance they are subject to misuse, since it is the Lord’s holy property. And Rami bar Ḥama, who raises the dilemma, holds that one cannot resolve it from here: where a gentile consecrated for a gentile to achieve atonement he does not raise the dilemma, for certainly they do not effect substitution. When he raises the dilemma, it is where a gentile consecrated for a Jew to achieve atonement, to discharge the Jew’s obligation: do we follow the one who consecrated, and the one who consecrated is a gentile, who does not effect substitution; or do we follow the one achieving atonement, who is a Jew, and he effects substitution?
rashi:b12.1: This is the reading: “Resolve it from what Rabbi Abbahu said”: below.
rashi:b12.2: One who consecrates adds one-fifth: if he wishes to redeem his consecrated animal, for example because a blemish developed in it, he can redeem it, and he adds one-fifth; but one who substitutes does not add one-fifth, as it is written: “And if he that consecrated it [will redeem it]” (Leviticus 27): for the first consecration you add one-fifth, and not for a second consecration such as a substitute. Another explanation: if he consecrated a house or a field and the owners came to redeem it, they do not redeem it without a fifth, as it is written (ibid.): “And if he that consecrated it will redeem it, then he shall add the fifth part”; but if another redeemed it, the Merciful One did not obligate him to give a fifth.
gershom:b9.1: One who consecrates adds one-fifth when he redeems his consecrated property.
rashi:b12.3: And the one achieving atonement effects substitution: if a Jew set aside an offering so that his fellow Jew would achieve atonement with it, and the one achieving atonement said, “This is in place of this,” his substitute is a substitute and he is flogged. Since it was set aside for his sake, we call it “his offering,” for we follow the one achieving atonement. So resolve [the dilemma] from this.
gershom:b10.1: And the one achieving atonement effects substitution: evidently we follow the one achieving atonement.
rashi:b12.4: And one who separates teruma: from his own grain for another’s untithed produce, to exempt it from the tithes.
